rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi reads v. 11 as extending v. 10: the creator of the heavens, earth, humanity and all creatures alone can be Lord, with no peer fit to be worshipped as his associate.
rows.anchor: It is God Who is the Creator of the heavens and the earth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The genitive pronoun in يذرؤ has no explicit word as antecedent; its referent is the idea that God created pairs and thereby established a system that continually produces and sustains them, a usage found in Arabic and earlier sūras.
rows.anchor: is not found in a specific word; it refers to the meaning which emanates

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The creator of the heavens, earth and the system producing human and animal pairs is peerless in being and attributes; nothing can be like Him.
rows.anchor: Nothing is like Him nor can anything ever be like Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since only God creates the heavens, earth, males and females, no other being can claim to have produced what comes from them or can be regarded as His peer.
rows.anchor: when no one other than God can be regarded as the creator of the heavens and the earth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The universe shows that God alone is peerless and truly hears and knows; His unmatched power and all-embracing knowledge enable Him to create and sustain it.
rows.anchor: it also reveals that He alone is the one Who really listens and knows.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because God hears everyone and knows everything, people should worship Him and ask Him alone for their needs; no means or intermediary is required.
rows.anchor: should worship Him and ask their needs from Him alone; He listens to all and knows everything

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The creator must also be master of the heavens and earth: their treasures are under His control, with rain descending and the earth yielding its stores at His direction; no deity shares in provision.
rows.anchor: Rain comes down at His bidding and the earth expels its treasure at His directive.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God distributes abundant or restricted livelihood according to knowledge and wisdom; He alone deserves gratitude, and people should hope and fear only Him, trusting that scarcity is neither ignorance nor injustice but wise and informed.
rows.anchor: he should not make this evil estimation that God has no knowledge of his circumstances or that He has done injustice to him

words: وَمَا وَصَّيْنَا بِهِۦٓ إِبْرَٰهِيمَ وَمُوسَىٰ وَعِيسَىٰٓ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Addressing Quraysh and Arabia, Islahi explains that the religion revealed to Muhammad is the same one enjoined on Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jesus: every prophet, from the first to the final, preached God's true religion, so it is not novel or alien.
rows.anchor: every prophet from the beginning to this final Prophet (sws) preached this very religion

words: وَمَا وَصَّيْنَا بِهِۦٓ إِبْرَٰهِيمَ وَمُوسَىٰ وَعِيسَىٰٓ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sequence names Noah and Muhammad first as the first and last prophets, then singles out Abraham, Moses and Jesus because pre-Qur’anic idolaters, Jews and Christians respectively claimed to follow them; it thus compresses prophetic history and highlights major communities.
rows.anchor: at the beginning, the first and last of them – Noah (sws) and Muḥammad (sws) – are mentioned.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The definite article in al-dīn, like that in al-kitāb, means God's religion; Islahi cites 3:19, which says the true religion before God is Islam.
rows.anchor: The religion of God has always been Islam as is mentioned in the following verse:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The religion's foundation is pure, complete monotheism, given to Noah and even Adam and revealed again to Muhammad; its beliefs and foundations remain the same, while differences lie only in sharīʿah's corollaries.
rows.anchor: The foundation of this religion is the pure and complete concept of monotheism.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Establishing religion requires sincere belief in its tenets and honest, righteous observance of its practical directives, with continuing care to prevent negligence and keep innovators from introducing changes.
rows.anchor: To establish religion means to sincerely believe in tenets which are meant to be believed in

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command against division presents religion as God's rope: everyone must cling to the true rope rather than accept another in its place, since breaking that bond leaves people with nothing to unite them.
rows.anchor: if one’s relation with this rope of God is broken, then the binding thread will be torn apart

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The idolaters addressed as finding the call burdensome are the Quraysh.
rows.anchor: refers to the idolaters of the Quraysh.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the call is worded generally, context shows it means monotheism, the point Quraysh idolaters most strongly resisted throughout the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: contextual indications show that they relate to monotheism.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's choosing assures the Prophet to be patient: His wise will and established practice prevail despite the Prophet's desire for their faith; He guides those who turn to Him, while others lose the urge for further guidance.
rows.anchor: He guides only those to Himself who themselves turn to Him for guidance.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition ilā after the verb for choosing indicates taḍmīn, a construction Islahi says he has explained elsewhere in the exegesis.
rows.anchor: shows that a taḍmīn occurs here.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earlier communities are rebuked for splitting through stubbornness after receiving divine knowledge; unlike a person stumbling in night darkness, those who err in clear daylight bear responsibility for their folly.
rows.anchor: even after being blessed with the light of divine knowledge they differed with each other merely because of stubbornness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Disputes among Jewish scholars and jurists resemble those among Muslims, but Muslims retain the Qur’an as a criterion, whereas Jews lost the Torah and had no means left to resolve their differences.
rows.anchor: this ummah has the Qur’ ān preserved with it. Hence it has a scale to judge between these differences

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jewish scholars' stubbornness and envy made them enemies of Jesus' followers; Christians later divided into sects, Paul deprived them of Torah and Gospel light, and Jews, Christians and Quraysh then tried to extinguish the Qur’an's light.
rows.anchor: Merely because of stubbornness and jealousy they became the enemies of the followers of Jesus (sws).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi attributes Jewish hostility to resistance to transferring religious leadership to the Israelites and notes that the Quraysh's reasons for opposing Muhammad are clear from these sūras.
rows.anchor: they did not want the reins of religious leadership to be transferred to the Israelites

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cited description means communities began disputing after truth came because of their misdeeds and mutual hostility; God and His Messenger continued to guide them to the straight path.
rows.anchor: whichever ummah adopted the way of creating disputes and differences did so because of its own misdeeds and mutual enmity

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The stated fixed term means communities receive respite until truth is conclusively conveyed; this warns them and assures the Prophet that judgment would otherwise have come immediately.
rows.anchor: each ummah will be given a certain respite until the truth is conclusively conveyed to it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause about those inheriting the Book after earlier communities connects back to the preceding sentence; the intervening statement about judgment is parenthetical admonition.
rows.anchor: The sentence in between is parenthetical in nature and is meant for admonishment.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi connects the theme to 41:45: Moses received the Book, people disputed over it, judgment was delayed until the Lord's appointed term, and they remained in baffling doubt.
rows.anchor: This topic has been discussed in the following words in the previous sūrah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who inherited the Book are Jews receiving the Torah after their ancestors; because it contained discrepancies they were left in perplexing doubt and should have valued the Qur’an as a resolution, but opposed it from obstinacy and envy.
rows.anchor: refer to the difference of the Jews who became the recipients of the Torah after their ancestors

rows.speaker: Generally people
rows.claim: Islahi rejects the common interpretation that the Book inherited in this clause is the Qur’an, since the context gives no indication for that reading.
rows.anchor: Generally people have interpreted the word
